title: Run models and plot results
text:
Now we’ll fit multilevel meta-analytic models in the R package metafor (Viechtbauer 2010). This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/2 meta and review summary.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.
Given the non-independence structures in this data we will fit a series of models with increasingly complex random effects, particularly to control for phylogenetic similarity between prey species and to also deal with non-phylogenetic components of species identity. We’ll create a model guide to organize these models, as well as our subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses. These analyses include:
Note that instead of including habitat type, locomotion, or landform as categorical predictors, we used separate univariate (intercept-only) models on these subgroups of the data. In part this is to keep the code cleaner (the results are the same regardless) but also because in most cases there was only one factor level of these variables with sufficient data to estimate coefficients and we were not interested in testing for differences between factor levels.

title: Run models and plot results
text:
Set up model guide
Now let’s create all the combinations of models we want to run. The function data.table::CJ is similar to expand.grid and makes all combinations of the input vectors. We’ll do this in two steps to avoid having to filter out some combinations that we don’t have sample size to run.

Code# # Do the guide in 2 steps. We don't have enough data for class * habitat sub-analyses.
guide <- CJ(analysis_group = unique(dat.final$analysis_group),
            moderator = c("1", "log_mass"),
            class = c("Birds", "Mammals", "Reptiles", "All"),
            habitat_trait = "All",
            prey_range = c("All", "inside"),
            non_phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
            phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
            only_dominant_effect_size = c("yes", "no")
)
guide <- guide[!(moderator == "log_mass" & class != "All"), ]

guide2 <- CJ(analysis_group = unique(dat.final$analysis_group),
             moderator = "1",
             habitat_trait = c("locomotion_volant.non_volant", 
                               "locomotion_volant.volant", 
                               "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting.other",
                               "ground_or_burrow_resting_or_nesting.ground", 
                               "Foraging_habitat_ground.other",
                               "Foraging_habitat_ground.ground", 
                               "continent_island.island", 
                               "continent_island.mainland"),
             class = c("All"),
             prey_range = c("All"),
             non_phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
             phylo_species = c("yes", "no"),
             only_dominant_effect_size = c("no")
             )

guide <- rbind(guide, guide2)


Now we’ll add a unique ID that we’ll use to compare alternative random effects per model series (model_comparison_id). And we’ll formulate strings which we’ll evaluate as R code for our random effects (random_effect), to filter our dataset (exclusion) and for our fixed effect formula (formula):

Codeguide[, model_comparison_id := paste0("model_comp_", .GRP), 
      by = .(analysis_group, class, moderator, prey_range,
             habitat_trait, only_dominant_effect_size)]

guide[, random_effect := "list(~1|article_id/Effect_size_ID"]

guide[, random_effect := ifelse(non_phylo_species == "yes",
                                paste0(random_effect, ", ~1|scientificName"), 
                                paste0(random_effect))]
guide[, random_effect := ifelse(phylo_species == "yes",
                                paste0(random_effect, ", ~1|phylo_species)"),
                                paste0(random_effect, ")"))]
guide

# Formulate exclusion formula:
guide[, exclusion := paste0("analysis_group == '", analysis_group, "'",
                            " & habitat_trait == '", habitat_trait, "'")]
guide[class != "All", exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & class %in% '", class, "'")]

guide[prey_range == "inside", 
      exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & prey_range_primary == 'inside'")]
guide[prey_range == "All"]

#
guide.m1 <- merge(guide,
               unique(dat[, .(analysis_group, analysis_effect_size)]),
               by = 'analysis_group',
               all.x = T)
guide.m1[is.na(analysis_effect_size)]
guide.m1

#
guide.m1[only_dominant_effect_size == "yes", 
         exclusion := paste0(exclusion, " & dominant_effect_size == 'yes'")]

#
guide.m1[, formula := ifelse(moderator == "1",
                             "~ 1",
                             paste("~", moderator))]


guide.m1[, model_id := paste0("model_", seq(1:.N))]


The resulting guide will execute 1,232 models and looks like this. exclusion, random_effect, and formula are text strings that we will evaluate to filter dataset and run models.

Now we’ll filter out models for which we have insufficient sample size. We’ll do this by evaluating the exclusion strings as a subsetting operation on the dataset. We’ll be very generous with sample size inclusion criteria and will fit models if there are at least 2 observations for lnOR and SMD effect size analysis groups and 5 observations for models with a continuous moderator (body mass).

CodeNs <- list()
sub.dat <- c()

for(i in 1:nrow(guide.m1)){
  sub.dat <- dat.final[eval(parse(text = guide.m1[i, ]$exclusion))]
  
  Ns[[i]] <- sub.dat[, .(n_species = uniqueN(scientificName),
                    n_articles = uniqueN(Article),
                    n_obs = .N,
                    model_id = guide[i, ]$model_id,
                    analysis_group = guide[i, ]$analysis_group,
                    class = guide[i, ]$class)]
  Ns[[i]]$model_id <- guide.m1[i, ]$model_id
  
}
Ns <- rbindlist(Ns)

guide.m2 <- merge(guide.m1, 
               Ns[, .(n_species, n_articles, n_obs, model_id)], 
               by = "model_id")

# More than 2 observations:
guide.m2 <- guide.m2[n_obs > 2, ]

# and at least 5 for continuous
guide.m2 <- guide.m2[!(moderator == "log_mass" & n_articles < 5), ]

Now let’s look at the timeline of the last records of extinct populations attributed to cat predation and the estimated arrival times of cats at those locations. These are reported based on the following categories based on population’s estimated extinction year and estimated cat arrival year:

Extinction before the arrival of cats
Extinction overlaps arrival of cats
Extinction within 0-100 years of cat arrival
Extinction 101-200 years after cat arrival

          factor(sci_label,
                 levels = plot_dt[
                   order(Class, sci_label),
                   unique(sci_label)
                 ])
]

  xmin = min(x_id) - 0.5,
  xmax = max(x_id) + 0.5
), by = Class]

), by = Class]

issue <- plot_dt[`Scientific name` %in% c("Todiramphus cinnamominus", "Cryptoblepharus egeriae", "Lepidodactylus listeri"), ]

  # class separators

    linetype = "dashed",

    aes(x = sci_label,

        y = min_difference,

    aes(x = sci_label, xend = sci_label,

    linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    y = "Years between cat arrival and last record",
    x = NULL) +
  theme_lundy +

    legend.position = "none",

title: Introduction
text:
This tutorial walks readers through the analyses associated with:

Wallach, A.D., Pereyra, P., Cuervo, L.M.V., Nakagawa, S., Lundgren, E.J. et al. ‘When consensus procedes the evidence.’ In Submission.

This tutorial assumes a basic understanding of R.
Feel free to clone or download the repo to interact with the code and data directly or to simply follow along in this webpage.
Note that all analyses were conducted in .R scripts in the scripts/ folder of the repo.
Some of the messier data-munging steps (e.g., standardizing text, collapsing or expanding categories) is conducted in these scripts, especially in the scripts/1_data_mgmt/ directory.
The interactive material on this webpage focuses on the core analyses (mostly in scripts/2_analysis/) and has been copied from these scripts for clearer communication but the original scripts remain in the repo and can be evaluated instead if that is preferred.

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Now we’ll meta-analyze the quantitative articles that provided data usable for a meta-analysis. We’ll start by calculating effect sizes and then converting effect sizes to a common type for analysis based on our analysis groups. This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/1_data_mgt/5 clean meta-analysis that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.
We’ll then run a suite of models and choose the model with the best random effects. Finally, we’ll plot the resulting model estimates and conduct publication bias tests.

title: Prepare meta-analysis dataset
text:
Prepare environment
We’ll start by loading packages and some helper functions. The convert_effect_sizes function contains formulas to convert between effect sizes. The formulas were originally provided by Borenstein et al. (2021). The get_r function is a simple helper function for extracting the correlation coefficient (r) from the cor.test output.

Coderm(list = ls())

library("data.table")
library("metafor")

library("readxl")

library("rotl")
library("broom.mixed")
library("here")

source("scripts/functions/convert_effect_sizes.R") # This function converts between effect sizes

get_r <- function(x, y){
  out <- cor.test(x, y)
  return(out$estimate)
}

Calculate effect sizes
We’ll start by loading the raw extracted data. Given the heterogeneity in experimental designs, the raw data was collected in 3 separate spreadsheets based on the data structure required for each effect size type. We’ll load these into a list object:

We also have a separate file that gives analysis groups for each effect size—e.g., how to group effect sizes for each model. These groupings are also the scaffold for some of our sensitivity analyses (e.g., different degrees of lumping across different experimental treatment types).

title: Citation network
text:
In this page we will plot and analyze the citation network uncovered by following all claimant and non-claimant sources regarding the effects of cats on threatened wildlife.
Claimant sources are reviews that claimed that cats were a driver of endangerment and are treated separately than non-claimants, which included a systematic search in Web of Science along with opportunistic records found and a published systematic review (Wallach and Lundgren 2025).
This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/1 citation networks and bias.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
These effect size formulas are digitized in the function convert_effect_sizes which has them scripted into R code. The formulas are in a side car csv file in the repo located at ‘scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv’
Codesource("scripts/functions/convert_effect_sizes.R")

formulas <- fread("scripts/functions/conversion_formulas.csv")
We’ll show the formulas below and demonstrate the use of the function. Note in all cases we will demonstrate with Cohen’s d (an uncorrected estimator of SMD). The function automatically converts Cohen’s d to Hedges’ g, which is the effect size estimator used in our analyses and returned by default from escalc.

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
SMD → lnOR
Let \(yi_{lnOR}\) and \(yi_{d}\) be the point estimate for the lnOR and Cohen’s d effect sizes and \(vi_{lnOR}\) and \(vi_{d}\) be their sampling variances:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_{lnOR} = yi_d * \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{3}} \\
&vi_{lnOR} = vi_{d} * \frac{\pi^2}{3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "lnOR",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the continuous data has a logistic distribution. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with `metafor::escalc` package defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g')

      <num>      <num>
1: 1.677835 0.03289868

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
lnOR → SMD
To convert from lnOR (\(yi_{lnOR}\)) to Cohen’s \(d\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = yi_{lnOR} * \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\
&vi_d = vi_{lnOR} * \frac{3}{\pi^2} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "lnOR",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes that the response variable is a discretized version of a continuous variable 
with a logistic distribution for each group (which approximates the normal distribution).
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses with and without converted data. 


   yi_trans    vi_trans
      <num>       <num>
1: 0.482765 0.003039636

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
SMD → Zr
To convert from SMD to Zr, we first convert \(d\) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and then to Zr, using a correction factor \(a\) for cases where \(n_1 \neq n_2\). Let \(yi_{Zr}\) and \(yi_d\) be the point estimate for Zr and Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a = \frac{(n_1 + n_2)^2}{n_1*n_2} \\
&r = \frac{yi_d}{\sqrt{yi_d^2 + a}} \\
&r \leftarrow \min(1, \max(-1, r_i))\\
&yi_{Zr} = atanh(r)\\
\end{aligned}
\]
And the sampling variance of Zr (\(vi_{Zr}\)): \[
\begin{aligned}
&n = n1 + n2 \\
&vi_{Zr} = \frac{1}{(n - 3)} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "SMD",
                     to = "Zr",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n1 = 15,
                     n2 = 15)

This conversion assumes a continuous variable was dichotomized to create the treatment and control groups. 
Note that the 'vi' is assumed to have been calculated with 'metafor::escalc' defaults (variance of 'd' not 'g'). 
Like usual, be careful :) 


    yi_trans   vi_trans
       <num>      <num>
1: 0.4474395 0.03703704

title: Appendix: effect size conversion formulas
text:
Zr → SMD
First, convert the point estimate of Zr (\(yi_{Zr}\)) to the correlation coefficient \(r\) and calculate the variance of \(r\) (\(vi_r\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&r = tanh(yi_{Zr}) \\
&vi_r = \frac{(1-r^2)^2}{(n-1)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Then calculate the point estimate (\(yi_d\)) and variance (\(vi_d\)) of Cohen’s d:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&yi_d = \frac{2*r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \\
&vi_d = \frac{4*vi_r}{(1-r^2)^3} \\
\end{aligned}
\]
In R:

Codeconvert_effect_sizes(from = "Zr",
                     to = "SMD",
                     yi = 0.9,
                     vi = 0.01,
                     n = 50)

'yi' is assumed to be 'Zr' (r-to-z transformed correlation coefficient). 
It may be preferable to supply 'r' and 'n' instead. To do so specify 'r' in the 'from' argument and provide a vector of correlation coefficients named 'r'. 
This conversion assumes that the underlying data was continuous with a bivariate normal distribution, with the two groups created by dichotomozing one of the two variables. 
Please use conversions carefully and conduct sensitivity analyses

title: Publication bias tests
text:
Given that some of our analysis contain mixed effect sizes we elected to only conduct time-lag publication bias tests. Other publication bias tests (e.g., small sample size) require uniform measurements of effective sample size or variance and are not suitable for original effect size types.
Time lag publication bias tests asks if significant effects have declined (or increased) since initial discovery, which is common when strong initial findings spur the development of a field. We thus regress our effect sizes against publication year. We’ll do a similar approach with a model guide as we did above. Except we’ll put all of the code into a single code block. This workflow is derived from a full R script in scripts/2_analysis/3 publication bias.R that includes additional checks and tests and is fully interactive if you clone the repo.

rma_predictions <- function(m, 
                            newgrid,
                            has_intercept = T){
  
  
  if(!is.data.frame(newgrid)){errorCondition("ERROR newgrid must be a data frame")}
  #create the new model matrix. 
  
  if(!all(unlist(lapply(names(newgrid), # lapply through names of newgrid to check that they're in formula
                        function(x) grepl(pattern=x,
                                          x = as.character(m$formula.mods)[-1]))))){
    errorCondition("ERROR: variables in newgrid are not in model formula")
  }
  
  
  # Drop levels that might be missing from the model...
  cols <- names(newgrid)
  coef_nms <- names(coef(m))
  temp <- c()
  
  if(has_intercept == F){
    
    for(i in 1:length(cols)){
      if(class(unlist(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F])) %in% c("factor", "character")){
        temp <- paste0(names(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F]),
                       unlist(newgrid[, cols[i], with = F]))
        newgrid <- newgrid[temp %in% coef_nms, ]
      }
    }
    
  }
  
  newgrid
  
  # Create prediction matrix
  predgrid <- (model.matrix(m$formula.mods, data=newgrid))
  predgrid
  
  if(any(grepl("intercept", colnames(predgrid), 
               ignore.case = TRUE))){
    #if intercept is present, remove it?
    predgrid <- predgrid[, -1]
  }
  
  # predict onto the new model matrix
  pred.out <- as.data.frame(predict(m, newmods=predgrid))
  
  #attach predictions to variables for plotting
  final.pred <- cbind(newgrid, pred.out)
  
  return(final.pred)
}
